# ESP-KVM

> An open-source IP-KVM: firmware that turns a ~$40 ESP32-P4 board and a TC358743
> HDMI bridge into a KVM-over-IP. It captures a target machine's HDMI, presents
> itself to that machine as a USB keyboard and mouse, and serves both to a browser
> over HTTPS - enough to reach a machine with no working OS (a BIOS screen, a boot
> menu, a kernel that will not come up). Free and open source, Apache-2.0.

Key facts:

- Hardware: an ESP32-P4 plus a TC358743 HDMI-to-MIPI-CSI-2 bridge. Reference build
  is a Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH with a Geekworm C790; a dozen other P4 boards have
  their own images, among them the Espressif ESP32-P4 Function EV Board. The one
  exception to the bridge is the M5Stack Unit PoE-P4, whose Add-on Display In
  carries a Lontium LT6911D instead - that add-on fits M5Stack's own units and
  nothing else.
- Video: follows the target's resolution automatically (a 640x480 BIOS through a
  1080p desktop); MJPEG or hardware H.264.
- Input: a composite USB HID device - keyboard, absolute and relative pointer,
  media keys.
- Text screens can be read back as characters: a BIOS, a boot loader or a console
  can be selected with the mouse and copied, or copied whole. Not OCR - the
  characters are read from the character grid the firmware draws them on, so a
  reading is either exact or refused. Graphical UEFI setups have no grid and are
  not read.
- The device can watch a text screen while nobody is connected: give it phrases
  (`no boot device`, `kernel panic`) and it raises an alert, in its log and in
  Home Assistant, when one appears. Off by default.
- Runbooks: a script of keys to send and phrases to wait for (`wait Press F2`,
  `key f2`), run on the device itself so it carries on with the browser closed;
  each one is a button in Home Assistant. Macros are the same language without
  the waits, played by the console. The language: https://espkvm.io/scripts/
- A scheduler: five-field cron lines that fire an action on the device on a
  timetable - Wake-on-LAN, an ATX button, a runbook, or a restart, and recording
  or a timelapse. The device sets its clock over SNTP (a LAN time server works
  with no internet) or takes the browser's time when you sign in; the time zone
  is picked from a list of cities in Settings.
- Push notifications: when a watched phrase appears or the screen goes blank,
  the device sends a message to Telegram (with a screenshot on the MJPEG codec)
  or to a webhook. Off by default.
- Pasting text types it out as keystrokes, so it follows the target's keyboard
  layout: US English, Russian, Czech, Ukrainian and Lithuanian. A character the
  layout cannot type is reported rather than guessed at.
- Recording: a button writes the screen to the device's own microSD card as H.264
  in .ts files - the same stream the viewers get, so nothing is encoded twice -
  and another saves a JPEG. A dashcam keeps the last minutes of the screen (in
  PSRAM, or on the card on boards short of it) and saves them as an MP4 with a
  chapter per event when the screen stays one flat colour, a watched phrase
  appears, the target's power LED goes off, or the operator asks; with
  notifications on the clip goes to Telegram as a video. Keystrokes can be
  written into a .srt beside the video, masked as dots by default. A timelapse
  keeps one frame every few seconds and plays back at 25 fps. Recordings play in
  the console, streamed from the card, and what the screen said during a
  recording is searchable (character screens only). Recording needs H.264 and a
  writable card.
- Virtual media: boot the target from a disk image on a microSD card or from a
  small image in the device's own flash.
- Networking: Ethernet, or WiFi on boards with an ESP32-C6 (the Function EV Board) -
  station or the device's own access point, one link at a time. A rescue hotspot and
  a captive portal keep a device reachable, and set up from a phone, when its network
  is out of range. mDNS (espkvm.local), DHCP or static addressing, and IPv6
  alongside IPv4 (autoconfigured from the router, nothing to fill in).
- An optional status screen on the device (I2C OLED, or a round SPI LCD) shows the
  link, address, capture state and health with no browser. The round one also shows
  a code a phone scans to join the rescue hotspot, and fills a ring while the
  recovery button is held. Either can be mounted upside down and turned over in
  the settings.
- Security: HTTPS with a certificate the device issues itself, plus a login. It is
  not meant for the public internet - keep it on a trusted network, or reach it over
  the built-in WireGuard client (split-tunnel, generates its own key).
- Updates install over the network into a spare slot, with rollback. The console
  shows the version and state of both slots and can boot the other one on demand.
  The device never reaches the internet on its own.
- It builds on jrowny/p4kvm, which brought up the TC358743 on the ESP32-P4 first.
